metadata.title: Oncology Pharmaceuticals: Streamlined Nonclinical Safety Studies for Biologics and Conjugated Products: Draft Guidance

candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 35 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 36 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 37 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended but 38 not required. 39
candidates.context: Recommendations (August 2019). 6 This guidance does not address nonclinical safety 32 assessments for impurities or excipients. 33

candidates.statement: Sponsors may propose alternative approaches for a 3-month general toxicology study for product 64 classes not described in this guidance, provided such approaches are sufficient to address product 65 safety. Such approaches for a 3-month general toxicology study may include a non-sacrificial 66 toxicology study, an alternative study design to reduce animal numbers, or a weight of evidence 67 (WoE) risk assessment for products with well-understood targets to replace an animal study. 68 These approaches could be supplemented with new approach methodologies (NAMs), as 69 appropriate. Sponsors proposing alternative approaches not specifically addressed in this 70 guidance should provide appropriate scientific justification and relevant supporting data. The 71 Agency will consider whether the alternative approach is adequate to characterize the safety risks 72 in each case. Sponsors are encouraged to discuss proposed alternative approaches with FDA 73
candidates.context: Current guidances for oncology pharmaceuticals support approaches to streamline nonclinical 49 testing. For instance, ICH S9 (March 2010) states “[i]n certain circumstances, determined case- 50 by-case, alternative approaches can be appropriate (e.g., for genotoxic drugs targeting rapidly 51 dividing cells, a repeat dose toxicity study in one rodent species might be considered sufficient, 52 provided the rodent is a relevant species).” The FDA guidance Oncology Therapeutic 53 Radiopharmaceuticals: Nonclinical Studies and Labeling Recommendations (August 2019) 54 recommends a risk assessment, instead of an animal toxicology study, to evaluate toxicities 55 associated with radioactive drugs, stating “[a] general toxicology study with the 56 radiopharmaceutical usually is not warranted. candidates.statement: • For biologics, animal toxicology studies should use pharmacologically relevant species. 84 Pharmacology studies should demonstrate binding of the oncology pharmaceuticals to 85 molecular target(s) and elicit the intended pharmacologic effects. In the absence of a 86 pharmacologically relevant species, the safety assessment could be based on a WoE risk 87 assessment in lieu of animal toxicology studies . 88
candidates.context: • For biologics that have pharmacological activity similar to humans in both rodent and 90 non-rodent species, general toxicology (1- and 3-month) studies may be conducted in a 91 single rodent species and supplemented with a WoE risk assessment, as appropriate. 92

candidates.statement: • For antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) with cytotoxic payloads, when the safety of the 102 payload is well-characterized (e.g., same payload as in approved ADCs) and the payload 103 is the main driver of toxicities, the 3-month toxicology study may be conducted in 104 rodents only, irrespective of ADC binding to the target antigen. The rodent study may use 105 the ADC or the payload, as appropriate. When the target of the antibody is novel and 106 binding to the target does not occur in the rodent species, a WoE risk assessment should 107 also be submitted. 108
candidates.context: • For CD3 bispecific T-cell engagers, an assessment of products’ chronic effects may be 99 based on a WoE risk assessment in lieu of a 3-month toxicology study. 100 B. Weight of Evidence Risk Assessment 110
